E1442.summary: The essence drawn out by the work: the celestial soul or arising Spirit of universal nature, identified with Mercury, the Elixir of Life, the Free Ether and Lumen Vestimenti.
E1442.body:
Atwood treats the Quintessence as no mere speculation: “that elder Quintessence of the magi which they introduce, not as a being of speculation merely, but of experimental science” [I.2 ¶16], obtainable as a compact, tangible essence. In the same passage she reports other names for it: the Kabalists' “Lumen Vestimenti, the Vehicle of Light”, and “the Greeks, the Free Ether, that is to say, freed from the prison of gross matter” [I.2 ¶16].

It is identified with the soul: “the quintessence is no other than our viscous celestial and glorious soul drawn from its minera by our magistery” [I.2 ¶33]; Synesius is quoted to the same effect, “the Quintessence and hidden thing of our Stone is nothing else than our viscous celestial and glorious soul” [III.1 ¶70]. It is also “This Proteus, then, or Mercury, or quintessence of philosophers” [I.2 ¶37], and a name of the whitened stage: “which, whitening, is called milk, dew, quintessence” [I.2 ¶40].

In the method it is the new life elicited from the crucifixion of the old: “which life is a very real and pure Quintessence, the Mercury so much sought after, even the Elixir of Life” [III.1 ¶49]. After seven repetitions comes “the final resurrection of the Quintessence into a permanent form of life” [I.3 n40]. Atwood says Hermes calls by this name “the arising Spirit of the Universal nature which, persisting separately, bounds as it were, by an invisible summit, every corporeal subsistence” [III.2 ¶36]. An adept reads “the dust of the earth” as “the arising quintessence of the universal nature” [I.3 n51].

It must be handled gently: Vaughan calls it “the sweet spirit of Peace, the true eternal Quintessence”, which “will depart from the elements, leaving both of them and thee to confusion” [III.4 ¶44]. A passage of uncertain voice (possibly the author of The Triumph) directs one to “convert and congeal the new-born Quintessence or mercurial water into an incombustible fixed unguent” [IV.2 ¶6]. Artephius credits his long life to “the use of this admirable quintessence” [I.1 ¶36].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “As man was the Quintessence of the whole creation, so woman was the Quintessence of man --- the love-spirit was in her” [APP ¶72]; and of the lower spherical quintessences, “these world forms are unstable and, uninformed with the Light Essential, resolve and die” [APP ¶23].

E1443.summary: Phrase from Hermolaus Barbarus's gloss on the divine water, describing it as of the nature of the ether and quintessence of things.
E1443.body: Quoted from Hermolaus Barbarus, who glosses the divine water as “a spirit of the nature of the ether and quintessence of things” [I.1 ¶20]. The grammar leaves it unclear whether the water is the quintessence of things or only of its nature.

E1444.summary: What is found when the elements of the compound creature are divided; further opened, it yields the angelical spirit.
E1444.body: In a quoted adept's counsel: “divide the elements, and you shall find the quintessential nature” [II.3 ¶52]; opened further, this nature yields the angelical spirit. Atwood also speaks of the son as the quintessential nature concentrated [I.3 n40].

E1445.summary: Author cited as containing allusions that support the story of Lully.
E1445.body: Cited by Atwood as containing allusions supporting the Lully story [I.1 ¶47].

E1446.summary: Rabbi cited from the Zohar on man as the Celestial Prototype and on the dew of light shaken from the hidden head.
E1446.body: Atwood cites the Rabbi (from the Zohar) approvingly for the doctrine of man as Celestial Prototype and image of God: “The Form of man, says the Rabbi Ben Jochai, contains all that is in the heaven and earth” [II.1 ¶42; II.1 n38]; he reads 'The Eternal has founded the earth upon his wisdom' as referring to the human prototype. Under the spelling “Rabbi Ben Jocahi” he is cited for the white form of the hidden principle and the dew of light: “From his head he shakes a dew which awakens the dead” [III.2 ¶3; III.2 n4].

E1447.summary: Voice of the Zohar cited for Thought as the hidden Principle unfolding into Spirit and articulate voice, which Atwood takes up as her theme.
E1447.body: Atwood quotes: “Thought is the Principle of all that is; but it is as first Unknown and shut up in itself.” [III.3 ¶78; III.3 n50]. She takes up this account of Thought unfolding into Spirit or Intelligence and articulate voice as her theme, calling it a 'Magnificent, yet impervious assertion'.

E1448.summary: The dissolution the operator enters once self-will and the other vices have been removed from his mind.
E1448.body: Atwood requires that self-will and the other vices “be removed from the mind of him who is to enter into the radical dissolution of Life” [IV.1 ¶40].

E1449.summary: Something discovered and set free through the adepts' theory once the superfluities are discharged.
E1449.body: Atwood speaks of “the medium by which the radical element is discovered and set free to the accomplishment of its inclusive law” [I.3 n4], once the superfluities are discharged. Elsewhere the 'radix' is to appear under the moist fire [I.3 ¶10]; the text does not explicitly link the two.

E1450.summary: What the prophet Enoch beheld in the Place to which he was snatched up, paired with the mystical Adamic Soil.
E1450.body: Atwood mentions “what he beheld of the Radical Essence, and the manifold glories of that mystical Adamic Soil” [III.2 ¶12], of the prophet (Enoch) snatched up to that Place.

E1451.summary: In Eudoxus, the body's essential moisture, consumed by common calcination but preserved and increased by philosophic calcination.
E1451.body: Quoted from Eudoxus: common calcination “consumes the greatest part of its radical humidity” [IV.3 ¶16], whereas philosophic calcination preserves and increases it. In the Fourth Key the earth is moistened with its own humidity [IV.3 ¶16].

E1452.summary: The substance of which metals are uniformly composed, which can be withdrawn from inferior forms and pass into a more perfect form.
E1452.body: Atwood equates it with the metals' subject-matter: “the subject-matter of these metals, the radical moisture of which they are uniformly composed” [I.2 ¶4]; it can be withdrawn from inferior Forms. Under a fermentive test it passes into a more perfect Form: “The radical moisture of the metal likewise, obeying the fermentive virtue of such a test when applied” [III.2 n38]. Khunrath is quoted that the Stone benefits metals “by transference of their radical moisture” [IV.3 ¶28], removing their terrestreity; this is not further defined.

E1453.summary: In Sendivogius, what remains after the philosophers' water consumes the gold and silver.
E1453.body: Quoted from Sendivogius: what remains ('the tenth part with one part') after the philosophers' water consumes the gold and silver — “this shall be the radical moisture of the metals” [IV.3 ¶21].

E1454.summary: The homogeneous root substance of all things, whose homogeneity is the ground of transmutation.
E1454.body: Atwood grounds transmutation in “the homogeneity of the radical substance of things” [I.2 ¶3].

E1455.summary: In Geber, the true root of the science, found only by a subtly searching mind.
E1455.body: Quoted from Geber: those without a subtly searching mind “cannot find the true Radix of this most precious science” [III.4 ¶3].

E1456.summary: A connection by which one in this state meets the whole image-world of his sphere; the change to a spiritual body comes by divine rapport.
E1456.body: Atwood writes that “each by rapport in this state becomes conversant with the whole phantasmagoric universe of his sphere” [II.3 ¶22], and that one “is changed from an earthly to a spiritual body, by rapport divine” [II.3 ¶29].

E1457.summary: The operation which, repeatedly passed through, alters the Vital Spirit and dissolves the whole natural born hypostasis.
E1457.body: Atwood: “a true Rational Analysis, which, repeatedly passed through, leads on to a dissolution of the whole natural born hypostasis” [III.1 ¶50]. Elsewhere 'the mode of analysis' is said to be directed by the Passive Understanding [III.1 ¶40]; the text does not explicitly link the two phrases.

E1458.summary: That by which the Matter returns in the Freed Will to consciousness and manifests the Supreme Cause.
E1458.body: Atwood speaks of the Matter “returning by its Rational Boundary in the Freed Will to consciousness” [III.2 ¶60], so manifesting the Supreme Cause. Not further explained.

E1459.summary: The pure aurific seed of Light hidden in ordinary life, represented by Cadmus, Jason, Orpheus and Aeneas; also named Perscrutinator.
E1459.body: Atwood names the Rational Ferment (also called Perscrutinator) as something “concerning which it will be our purpose to inquire hereafter” [I.3 n32]. In myth it is represented by heroes; of Cadmus: “identified him with Jason, Orpheus, Aeneas, and the rest, who represent the Rational Ferment;” [III.1 ¶66]; the other faculties of the mind are originally attendant on it. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she explains why the principium is hard to find: “the rational ferment, the pure aurific seed of Light, is hidden in this life of ours” [APP ¶35].

E1460.summary: The inbred form according to which the Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature to itself.
E1460.body: Atwood: the Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature to itself “according to the Rational Form inbred” [IV.3 ¶29].

E1461.summary: The strongest of lights, the One Leader which, discovered and set in motion, actuates the Spirit to overcome the corporeal; also the aurific seed.
E1461.body:
Atwood: “The Rational Light, once discovered and set in motion, actuates the Spirit” [III.3 ¶23], which then overcomes the corporeal. It is the sole deliverer of the veiled spirit: “there is but One Leader, who should undertake the deliverance; one only, we repeat; he that is allied --- the same Rational Light” [III.4 ¶19]; strengthened in practice, it is raised to the 'allegoric siege of life' and kindled to overcome the stronghold of evil there.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): Saturn must be satiated from without with plenty “of the honey of the bees", the aurific seed, the Rational Light” [APP ¶72]; “The Rational Light is the strongest of all lights, and overcomes every other.” [APP ¶168], and once realized all life orders itself round it, constituting re-integration of being. In the inner combat it acts last: deprived of its understanding essence, “the rational intellect goes forth to avenge it and die” [APP ¶153].

E1462.summary: Something moved about by the Almighty force, set beside the image of an established monarch whom inferior powers follow.
E1462.body: Atwood mentions “the Almighty force that moves about the Rational Magnet” [II.4 ¶38], alongside the image of an established monarch followed by the inferior powers. Not further defined.

E1463.summary: In Porphyry, that which is present with a man himself; being present with it, and absent from externals, is presence with true Being.
E1463.body: Quoted from Porphyry (spelled 'Prophyry'): one should be “present with that which is present with himself, that is to say, with his rational part” [III.2 ¶59]; such presence, with absence from the external, is presence with true Being.

E1464.summary: The way, by reflexive analysis of the analyzer, of penetrating through Nature's Understanding into her Causal Light.
E1464.body: Atwood, of reflexive analysis of the analyzer: “this is the way of rational permeation, by the Understanding of Nature, into her Causal Light” [IV.1 ¶20].

E1465.summary: Reason's inquiry that proves all things, rejecting the false and holding the true; better called discrimination, and required of the Hermetic Student.
E1465.body: Atwood distinguishes it from its mock ally: “Rational skepticism has quite another object and never exhibits itself in the refractory form of its mock ally.” [III.4 ¶15]. It proves all things, rejecting the false and holding the true, and is required of the Hermetic Student: “Such skepticism, more properly perhaps called discrimination” [III.4 ¶15].

E1466.summary: In Sendivogius, the reasons of life and understanding in fire, infused by God into man, by which alone he differs from other creatures and resembles God.
E1466.body: Quoted from Sendivogius: “This soul was of that most pure fire, infused by God into the vital spirit” [II.4 ¶39]; “In it are the reasons of life and understanding, which are distributed in the first infusion of man’s life, and these are called the rational soul” [II.4 ¶39]. By it alone man differs from other creatures and is like God. A Latin line of unclear voice reads “Deus nunquam creavit rem nobiliorem sub coelo praeter animam rationalem” [III.3 ¶81] (ours: God never created a nobler thing under heaven except the rational soul); per this rendering it is ranked against 'our Mercury', but the reading is uncertain.

E1467.summary: Voice of the Famma et Confessio, cited to illustrate philosophers visiting the Elysian place.
E1467.body: Cited from the Famma et Confessio to illustrate philosophers visiting the Elysian place: “Vidi aliquando Olympicos domos” [II.4 ¶11; II.4 n5] (ours: I once saw the Olympic houses).

E1468.summary: The state in which all life moves orderly round the realized Rational Light.
E1468.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), once the Rational Light is realized and all life orders itself round it: “This constitutes the re- integration of being” [APP ¶168], called there 'the manifestation of the **** in man'.

E1469.summary: The superior, supernatural ruling principle in man, temple of the Deity, which as ferment gathers all into its Light; called Wisdom, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture.
E1469.body:
Atwood makes Reason the rightful ruler of the soul, around which the inferior powers settle; in this life it is hidden and latent. One “will so venerate this Reason” [II.4 ¶36], and she names it: “This is the Sal Sepientum et Mercurius Philosophorum” [II.4 ¶39]. It is the dwelling of Deity: “God dwells, says the Jew Philo, in the rational part of man as in a palace” [II.1 ¶43]; “For this Reason is her temple wherein the Eternal Self-existent dwells” [II.1 ¶50]; and “Reason, which is, as it were, the temple of that Intellectual Ilumination” [III.1 ¶5], entered through the phantasic vestibule.

The superior, supernatural Reason (of which natural reason is the image) works as ferment: “this Reason gaining the ascendancy, would gather all up, as a ferment, into the superior essence and traction of her own Light” [III.1 ¶21], separating false forms and assimilating the inferior life. “It is of this the ancients speak, calling it Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture”; “For it is Light indeed, and an occult splendor of existence transcendentally pure”; it is conceived as “the Intellectual sun” [III.1 ¶21].

It is the one universal faculty consciously distinguishable by itself: “this root of reason which is truly catholic”; “in our mere individual consciousness it is the foundation of all law” [III.1 ¶23]; cut off from its source it is weak and unaware of it. Completed by the work, “reason BECOMING A BRIGHT Light in the periphery of her fiery essence remains immortal, and is the Mistress of Life” [III.3 ¶80], “leaving reason nothing more to doubt of” [III.3 ¶82].

In practice it is man's “especial prerogative of Reason and rectitude of purpose” [IV.4 ¶12], with “the Reason also, purified and singled out by Art for the encounter” [IV.4 ¶9]. The upright mind submits to the universal Rule, “including all in the catholic perceivance of this Reason”: “let him search for the Root of Reason rationally, and hold by it, and conspire with It” [IV.4 ¶32].

E1470.summary: A principle with stolen forces provoking conflict in life, whose identical representative the Divine Art requires so those forces can be drawn forth and spent.
E1470.body: Atwood describes a rebellious Principle whose 'stolen forces' provoke a bloody conflict in life; the Divine Art requires an identical representative of him so those forces may be drawn forth and spent. Egyptian relics show “innumerable similitudes belonging both to this rebellious Principle and to that identical representative of him which the Divine Art requires” [III.1 ¶64], depicted in human semblance between foes.

E1471.summary: The recipes of mercenary pretenders, which led people into error and crime.
E1471.body: Atwood blames mercenary pretenders for error and even “the commitment even of egregious crimes by their receipts” [I.1 ¶64].
